title: Someone is hurt or sick
short: First aid for bleeding, burns, breathing, injuries and sudden illness
intro: Find the right first-aid pages fast when someone is injured or suddenly ill and help may be slow to arrive. Start with checking the person and the scene, then pick what you see. These pages describe what trusted first-aid manuals say; they do not replace training or a medical professional.

choices.label: I don't know what's wrong – how do I check the person?
choices.hint: Accident, collapse, several injured people, you need a calm order of steps

read.label: Stay calm, make the place safe, check breathing then bleeding
read.note: Hesperian's step-by-step start for any emergency: calm yourself, move away from danger, check breathing first, then heavy bleeding, and protect yourself from blood.

read.label: Check the whole body and keep re-checking
read.note: How to look head to toe for hidden injuries, comfort the person, give helpers jobs and keep watching because injured people can suddenly get worse.

read.label: The general approach: scene safety and life threats first
read.note: IFRC 2025 guidelines on keeping yourself safe, then finding life-threatening problems (unresponsive, breathing, severe bleeding) before anything else. Written for first-aid educators.

read.label: The ABCDE check: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure
read.note: WHO/ICRC Basic Emergency Care explains the ABCDE order and why each problem is fixed before moving on. Course for frontline health workers; some actions need training.

choices.label: Bleeding, a cut or a wound
choices.hint: Heavy bleeding, deep cut, tourniquet, dirty wound, wound getting red or swollen

read.label: Stop bleeding with direct, firm pressure
read.note: Raising the wound, pressing a folded clean cloth firmly on or into it, adding cloth instead of removing it, and how long to keep pressing on a large wound.

read.label: Video: direct pressure for life-threatening bleeding
read.note: American Red Cross demonstration (about 5 minutes, captions) of finding the source of bleeding, placing a dressing and pushing hard.

read.label: Clean every wound well
read.note: Why cleaning prevents infection, washing with plenty of flowing clean water, soapy water for dirty wounds, and flushing deep wounds.

read.label: Signs a wound is infected or spreading
read.note: Swelling, redness, heat, pus, bad smell; fever and swollen lymph nodes mean the infection is spreading. Next page covers sepsis danger signs.

choices.label: Does this wound need stitches or a doctor?
choices.hint: Gaping cut, graze, old wound, deep wound, tetanus worry

read.label: Caring for a wound and when to close it
read.note: Keeping wounds clean and covered, changing bandages, which wounds should be left open (including wounds over 12 hours old) and which heal better closed.

read.label: When a cut benefits from stitches
read.note: Which cuts benefit from stitches and an illustrated method; deep wounds that cannot be closed properly should be left open. Stitching is a skill to learn beforehand.

read.label: Cuts and grazes: clean, cover, and when to get care
read.note: IFRC 2025 guidance: clean with running water, cover the wound, seek help if not protected against tetanus or if signs of infection or fever appear.

choices.label: Burn or scald
choices.hint: Burnt or burned by fire, hot water, cooking oil, chemicals, electricity, electrocuted

read.label: Cool the burn with running water
read.note: IFRC 2025 key action and guidelines for heat and chemical burns, what to put on afterwards, and why not to break blisters.

read.label: When a burn needs emergency care
read.note: Burns that are large, deep, near the face, throat or genitals, or from chemicals, electricity or flames need emergency help; signs of burn infection; watching children for chilling.

read.label: Minor vs dangerous burns and the palm-size rule
read.note: Hesperian on cooling minor burns, recognising deep or large burns (using the person's palm as about 1% of the body) and care on the way to help.

choices.label: Broken bone, dislocation or sprain
choices.hint: Fall, twisted ankle, bruise, fractured or dislocated limb, looks bent or can't be moved, sling

read.label: Is it broken, dislocated or sprained?
read.note: How to tell these injuries apart and the advice to keep the part still and get help when you cannot tell.

read.label: Make a splint and a sling
read.note: Illustrated steps for splinting an arm, leg, thigh or finger with cardboard or board, and checking that fingers and toes stay warm with normal feeling.

read.label: Fractures, sprains and strains: keep it still
read.note: IFRC 2025: treat any limb injury as a possible fracture, stabilise it, cool for up to 20 minutes, and watch for bleeding and shock with thigh fractures.

read.label: Sprains, strains and bruises: rest, ice, compress, elevate
read.note: Signs of a sprain, the rest-ice-compression-elevation routine, how to wrap a bandage, and bruises that may signal something more serious.

choices.label: Not breathing, unconscious or choking
choices.hint: Collapsed or fainted, not responding, heart stopped (cardiac arrest), AED or defibrillator, can't breathe, gasping, food stuck in throat, drowning

read.label: Unresponsive and not breathing normally: start CPR
read.note: IFRC 2025: assume cardiac arrest if unresponsive with abnormal breathing, call for help, and start chest compressions. Continues on the next two pages with depth, ratio and steps.

read.label: Video: hands-only CPR
read.note: American Red Cross demonstration (about 3 minutes, captions) of checking the person, calling 911 and doing compression-only CPR.

read.label: Unresponsive but breathing: the recovery position
read.note: IFRC 2025 on keeping the airway open by turning the person on their side, and what to do differently if a spine injury is possible.

read.label: Choking: back blows and abdominal thrusts
read.note: Hesperian steps for an adult or child who cannot cough or talk, including pregnant or large people; next page covers babies under one year and drowning.

choices.label: Pale, cold, sweaty, weak – could be shock
choices.hint: After heavy bleeding, bad burns, severe vomiting or a severe allergy

read.label: Signs of shock and what to do on the way to help
read.note: Hesperian explains shock (not the same as being scared), its warning signs and first steps while getting help.

read.label: Shock: lie the person down and keep them at normal temperature
read.note: IFRC 2025 guidance on positioning, when leg raising is and is not appropriate, and getting emergency care immediately.

choices.label: Head, neck or back injury
choices.hint: Fall or fell, car crash, blow to the head, spinal or vertebral injury, fractured skull, spine or vertebrae, dislocated neck, confused or numb after an accident

read.label: Protect a possible spine injury
read.note: When to assume the spine is hurt, keeping neck and back still, signs of spine injury and a simple movement and feeling check.

read.label: Concussion vs severe brain injury
read.note: Signs of mild and severe brain injury, watching the person for 24 hours, and the signs that mean bleeding inside the skull needs immediate help.

read.label: Spinal injury: keep still, do not strap the neck
read.note: IFRC 2025: who may have a spinal injury, always call emergency services, and when an unresponsive person should or should not be moved.

read.label: Head injury: when to get emergency care
read.note: IFRC 2025 concussion screening questions and a list of warning signs after a blow to the head that need emergency medical care.

choices.label: Too hot or too cold (heat stroke, hypothermia, frostbite)
choices.hint: Heatstroke or heat wave, no AC, confused and hot, shivering, frostnip, numb white fingers

read.label: Heat illness: cool the person fast
read.note: IFRC 2025 on heat exhaustion and heatstroke, cooling methods, and when to call emergency services. Next page lists the warning signs.

read.label: Heat stroke: signs and how to cool someone
read.note: Hesperian on who is most at risk, dangerous signs and how to cool quickly; warns that ice baths are dangerous for older or ill people.

read.label: Hypothermia: warm gradually
read.note: IFRC 2025 on removing wet clothes, passive and active warming, avoiding burns from warm stones, and always getting medical help.

read.label: Frostbite: warming frozen fingers and toes
read.note: Hesperian on rewarming frozen parts, not rubbing, and why a thawed part must not refreeze. See the shelter topic for keeping a home warm or cool.

choices.label: Severe allergic reaction
choices.hint: Swollen lips or throat, trouble breathing or can't breathe, hives after a sting, food or medicine

read.label: Mild allergy vs anaphylaxis
read.note: Hesperian lists signs of a severe allergic reaction and when epinephrine is needed; next page shows where it is injected and other steps.

read.label: Help the person use their own epinephrine auto-injector
read.note: IFRC 2025 key action: stop contact with the allergen and help the person use prescribed medication. Next page covers calling EMS and repeat reactions.

choices.label: Snakebite
choices.hint: Bitten by a snake, rattlesnake, fang marks, venomous or harmless

read.label: IFRC: keep the person as still as possible
read.note: IFRC 2025 key action and steps: a sling for an arm, no walking on a bitten leg, the bite at or below heart level, and removing jewellery before it swells.

read.label: No tourniquet, sucking, cold compress, rubbing or cutting
read.note: IFRC 2025 caution: these may cause further harm. Also washing the wound and carrying the person when help is far away, and telling medical staff the type of snake.

choices.label: Animal or human bite
choices.hint: Dog, cat, bat or monkey bite, bitten by a person, rabies worry

read.label: IFRC: rinse the bite with clean water
read.note: IFRC 2025 key action: cleaning the bite as quickly as possible with clean water and soap, why bites get infected, and the risk of rabies.

read.label: When to get medical care after a bite
read.note: IFRC 2025: stopping any bleeding first, and getting care if the wound needs closing, for tetanus, for a wild animal bite where rabies is common, or signs of infection.

choices.label: Insect sting, tick, spider or jellyfish
choices.hint: Bee or wasp sting or stinger, ticks, mosquito or spider bite, scorpion, jellyfish or stinging fish

read.label: IFRC: removing a tick or a bee stinger
read.note: IFRC 2025 steps: a tick pulled out with tweezers close to the skin, a stinger scraped out with a flat object such as a bank card, then cleaning and cooling the area.

read.label: Jellyfish and stinging fish
read.note: IFRC 2025: rinsing with seawater, heated water for pain, removing stinging cells and tentacles without getting stung, and not rubbing.

read.label: Spider bites and scorpion stings
read.note: Hesperian: most spider bites and scorpion stings do not cause serious or lasting harm, keeping the part still, cold for pain, and signs that need medical help.

choices.label: Poisoning: swallowed a chemical, medicine or pesticide
choices.hint: Poisoned by a cleaning product, rat poison, too many pills (overdose), fuel, button battery, a child got into something

read.label: First steps for any poisoning
read.note: IFRC 2025 steps: stop the exposure, find out what was taken and how much, reach a poison centre or EMS and follow them. Do not make the person vomit.

read.label: Do not induce vomiting or give milk, water or charcoal
read.note: IFRC 2025: do not induce vomiting, and do not give milk, water or activated charcoal unless a poison centre or poison expert says to. Also lists signs of poisoning.

choices.label: Diarrhea, vomiting or dehydration
choices.hint: Diarrhoea, throwing up or threw up, puking, stomach bug, loose motions, bad water, baby or older person dehydrated or drying out

read.label: Signs of dehydration and when it gets worse
read.note: Hesperian on early dehydration signs, the signs it is getting dangerous (including the skin-pinch test) and why young children are at special risk.

read.label: Make a home rehydration drink
read.note: Hesperian recipe for salt and sugar or cereal rehydration drink, how to taste-check it, and how much to give after each stool.

read.label: Diarrhea in children: drinks, food, no plug medicines
read.note: Hesperian on how much rehydration drink to give small children, continuing food and breastfeeding, and avoiding anti-diarrhea medicines.

read.label: Danger signs with vomiting or diarrhea
read.note: Vomiting and diarrhea warning signs (blood, a lot of watery stool fast, weeks of diarrhea) and who is most at risk.

choices.label: Chest pain, stroke signs, seizure or diabetic emergency
choices.hint: Crushing chest pain or heart attack, face drooping, fit or convulsion, diabetic acting confused

read.label: Signs of a heart attack
read.note: Hesperian lists heart attack signs in men and women and first steps while getting help. Mentions medicines; check the source's precautions.

read.label: Stroke: face, arm, speech – get to a hospital fast
read.note: Hesperian on recognising a stroke and why treatment within the first hours matters.

read.label: What to do during a seizure
read.note: Clearing space, turning the person on their side, not holding them down, and the causes that need urgent medical help.

read.label: Low blood sugar in someone with diabetes
read.note: Hesperian on danger signs of low blood sugar, giving sugar if conscious, and when to get help if they do not improve.

choices.label: Phones are down or help is far away
choices.hint: Earthquake, many injured, no ambulance coming, need to send for help, stretcher

read.label: Signs a person is too sick to treat at home
read.note: Where There Is No Doctor (2025) list of signs of dangerous illness that mean skilled medical help is needed as soon as possible.

read.label: When and how to look for medical help
read.note: Bringing the health worker to the person or carrying them by stretcher, and sending a responsible messenger with a written patient report (form on the next page).

read.label: How responders set up treatment areas after a disaster
read.note: CERT manual on decentralized and central medical treatment areas where survivors are cared for until transport to professional care. Written for trained CERT volunteers.

read.label: Moving a badly injured person on a stretcher
read.note: Where There Is No Doctor (2025) illustration of lifting an injured person without bending them and keeping the head and neck still.

limits.text: Do not apply a tourniquet, suck out the venom, apply a cold compress, rub the bite or cut the wound after a snakebite; these may cause further harm.
Get emergency help at once if someone is bitten or stung in the mouth or on the throat; any swelling could block their airway.
Rabies is deadly once signs appear. After a monkey, bat or raccoon bite, or a bite from a dog or another animal that could have rabies, get medical care right away to decide on rabies vaccination.

If someone has heavy blood loss, cannot be woken, has great difficulty breathing, cannot drink for a day or more, or other listed danger signs, they are probably too sick to treat at home; seek skilled medical help as soon as possible.
Watch for confusion, a very fast heart rate, and cold, moist, pale skin after bleeding: these are danger signs of losing too much blood and shock.
A tourniquet is a last resort, for when you are willing to risk losing the limb to save a life: a limb that cannot be saved, or limb bleeding that direct pressure cannot slow.
After applying a tourniquet, get to a hospital as fast as you can; the limb is likely to be lost after 2 or 3 hours.
Emergency medical services should be called for all severe bleeding.
Signs of sepsis (fever or very low temperature, fast heart rate, fast breathing, confusion) mean an infection has spread: get medical help quickly.
Burns that are large, deep, on the face, throat or genitals, or caused by chemicals, electricity or flames need emergency medical services.

Deep burns, burns covering 10% or more of the body, burns on joints, face or genitals, and burns in children are dangerous: get help. Children should be cared for in a burn-equipped hospital whenever possible.
After a head injury, growing confusion, a worsening headache, passing out or a seizure suggest bleeding inside the skull and need immediate medical help.
Always call emergency services when a spinal injury is suspected; do not move an unresponsive person with a possible spine injury unless they are in danger or help has arrived.
Call emergency services for heat illness if the person shows unusual behaviour or confusion, becomes unresponsive, has a seizure or has a body temperature above 39°C (102.2°F).
For all cases of hypothermia, emergency medical services should be called and the person's airway, breathing and circulation watched.
Severe hypothermia (body temperature 32°C/90°F or less, unconscious, no longer shivering): handle the person as gently as possible while quickly getting them to help.
Call emergency services whenever anaphylaxis is suspected; symptoms can return hours after improving. Recognising anaphylaxis requires training.
Setting bones and putting on a cast should be done by someone with experience; keep a broken bone still until then.
If a child with dehydration does not start to improve quickly with rehydration drink, get help.
A suspected stroke needs a hospital right away; treatment works best within the first hours.
Do not make a poisoned person vomit, and do not give milk, water or activated charcoal unless a poison control centre or poison expert tells you to.
The Basic Emergency Care course is written for frontline health providers; airway devices and other practical skills in it require training.

prepare.label: What to keep in a home medicine and first-aid kit
prepare.note: Where There Is No Doctor (2025) home kit list with gloves, gauze, bandages, tape and other supplies, with page references for how each is used. Earlier pages explain caring for the kit.

prepare.label: FEMA basic emergency supply kit checklist
prepare.note: Ready.gov 2024 checklist including a first aid kit, whistle, dust mask and plastic sheeting; first page adds prescriptions, glasses and a first aid book.

prepare.label: CERT volunteer first aid pouch
prepare.note: CERT 2019 list of minimum first-aid pouch items (dressings, pads, triangular bandages, roller bandage) plus gloves, lights and tools on the previous page.

prepare.label: Red Cross field first aid bag and how to look after it
prepare.note: ICRC 2006 annex on keeping a first aid bag clean and restocked, improvising, and a detailed contents table. Written for Red Cross first aiders in conflict areas; older edition.

prepare.label: Take a first aid, CPR, Until Help Arrives or CERT course
prepare.note: FEMA Earthquake Safety at Home (2020) recommends a ready first aid kit and taking first aid, CPR, Until Help Arrives or CERT training.

prepare.label: Carry a card if you have diabetes and teach your family
prepare.note: Hesperian advice to wear a medical bracelet or card listing diabetes and medicines, and teach family the danger signs.

prepare.label: Allergy plan: carry the card and prescribed medication
prepare.note: IFRC 2025 prevention advice: avoid known allergens and make sure the person and caregivers know where their prescribed medication is.

learn.label: IFRC International First Aid Guidelines 2025
learn.note: Current evidence-based guidelines from the Red Cross Red Crescent, topic by topic with key actions. Written for first-aid educators and programme designers, so it is detailed.

learn.label: Where There Is No Doctor (2025): Chapter 10 First Aid
learn.note: The classic village health book's first aid chapter, including shock, bleeding, wounds, burns, fractures and moving injured people.

learn.label: Video: how to use a tourniquet
learn.note: American Red Cross demonstration (about 3 minutes, captions) of placing and tightening a windlass tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding.

learn.label: Video: the recovery position
learn.note: St John Ambulance demonstration (about 2.5 minutes, captions) of rolling an unresponsive, breathing person onto their side. UK emergency numbers are mentioned.

learn.label: Video: using an AED on an adult
learn.note: American Red Cross demonstration (about 3 minutes, captions) of turning on an AED, placing pads and following its prompts.

learn.label: Video: helping someone who is choking
learn.note: St John Ambulance demonstration (about 2.5 minutes, captions) of recognising choking, back blows and abdominal thrusts.

learn.label: Video: helping someone with heat exhaustion
learn.note: British Red Cross (about 3 minutes, captions): pale, cold, clammy skin and dizziness; shade, sitting down, sips of water; when to get medical advice or call the UK emergency number.

learn.title: First aid
learn.label: Encyclopedia: First aid (MDWiki)
learn.note: Medical encyclopedia overview of first aid; from there, linked articles cover bleeding, burns, CPR, shock and more. Reference reading, not step-by-step instructions.

learn.title: Simple triage and rapid treatment
learn.label: Encyclopedia: START triage, for trained responders (MDWiki)
learn.note: How trained responders sort many injured people into four color groups by walking, breathing, pulse and following commands. Reference reading, not training.

learn.title: Psychological first aid
learn.label: Encyclopedia: Psychological first aid (MDWiki)
learn.note: Medical encyclopedia article on how responders and volunteers support people right after a disaster: safety and comfort, listening without pressure, practical help and referral. Background reading, not training.
